title: Cheat Sheets
sub: One-page lookup tables for the shell, networking, HTTP, permissions, Python, pip, git and web development
goals: Look up a shell, zsh or networking command by task in under a minute
Read a subnet, port, status code or permission value straight from a table
Recall Python syntax, built-ins and venv commands without leaving the terminal
Copy a ready-made pipeline from the quick-recipes section and adapt it
Find a JavaScript, DOM, DevTools, Node.js, XPath or CSS idiom in seconds

blocks.text: This chapter is for lookup, not for reading front to back. Each section is one page of tables and short code blocks, ordered the way you reach for them: move around, shape text, edit the command line, test the network, then the reference numbers (ports, subnets, status codes, permissions) then Python, pip and git, and finally the web: JavaScript, the DOM, DevTools, Node.js and npm, XML and CSS. Nothing here is explained from scratch. When a row is unfamiliar, the link at the top of each section goes to the chapter that teaches it, and the Command Atlas has the full card.

Placeholders such as `{{file}}` and `{{host}}` are editable chips. Set them once and every copy button on this page uses your values. The lab files (`access.log`, `ips.txt`, `hosts.txt`, `users.csv`, `ping.log`, `scan.txt`) are the ones from [Setting up your lab](#setup).
Taught in [Working with files](#files). Paths: `/` root, `~` home, `.` here, `..` parent, `-` previous directory (`cd -`).

blocks.text: More that need your own machine (macOS network commands):

blocks.code:
# every IPv4 address configured on this Mac
ifconfig | awk '/inet / {print $2}'

# processes listening on TCP, with the program name
lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN | awk 'NR > 1 {print $1, $9}' | sort -u

# TCP connections per state
netstat -an -p tcp | awk 'NR > 2 {c[$6]++} END {for (s in c) print c[s], s}' | sort -rn

# the five biggest things in the current folder
du -sk * | sort -rn | head -5

# newest five files, long format
ls -lt | head -6

# HTTP status of each host in hosts.txt
while read -r h; do printf '%s ' "$h"; curl -s -o /dev/null -m 5 -w '%{http_code}\n' "https://$h"; done < hosts.txt

# average ping time from a 10-packet run
ping -c 10 {{host}} | awk -F'[/ ]' '/round-trip/ {print $8 " ms avg"}'

# which IPs does a domain resolve to, one per line
dig +short {{domain}} | grep -E '^[0-9.]+$'

blocks.text: `ping` summary lines differ by OS. On macOS the line is `round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 8.1/9.4/12.0/1.5 ms`; with `-F'[/ ]'` the average lands in field 8. Print the line and count fields before you trust a number.

blocks.text: Method for any prefix: block size = 256 minus the interesting octet of the mask (`/26` has mask octet 192, block size 64, so networks start at .0 .64 .128 .192). Check with Python:

blocks.code:
$ python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; n=i.ip_network('192.168.1.77/26', strict=False); print(n, n.network_address, n.broadcast_address, n.num_addresses)"
192.168.1.64/26 192.168.1.64 192.168.1.127 64

blocks.text: Reading `ls -l`: `-rwxr-xr-x@ 1 you staff 412 Oct  8 09:12 run.zsh`. The first character is the type (`-` file, `d` folder, `l` link), then nine permission bits. A trailing `@` means extended attributes (such as quarantine); `+` means an ACL (`ls -le` shows it). Default permissions come from the umask: `umask 022` gives new files 644 and new folders 755.

task.text: Without using the browser, find the broadcast address and the number of usable hosts for `192.168.1.77/26` using Python's `ipaddress` module, then check the usable-host count against the subnet table above.

hints: `ipaddress.ip_network(..., strict=False)` accepts a host address with a prefix.
blocks.solution: python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; n=i.ip_network('192.168.1.77/26', strict=False); print(n.broadcast_address, n.num_addresses - 2)"

why.text: The network is 192.168.1.64/26, so the broadcast address is 192.168.1.127 and there are 62 usable hosts. The table row for `/26` agrees.

blocks.title: A pipeline from the recipes

task.text: From `access.log` in `~/lab`, print the three client IPs with the most requests that returned 404, with counts. Start from the status histogram recipe and add a filter stage.

hints: Status is field 9 and the client IP is field 1.
blocks.solution: awk '$9 == 404 {print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

why.text: `awk` filters and projects in one stage, then the counting idiom `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` ranks the result. Swapping the filter condition gives you the same report for any status.

task.text: `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-x--x`. Write the octal mode, then the `chmod` command in symbolic form that would remove the group's execute bit from it.

why.text: Owner rwx is 7, group r-x is 5, other --x is 1. `g-x` clears only the group's execute bit and leaves the rest alone.

questions.q: Which mask does macOS `ifconfig` print for a /24?
questions.why: `ifconfig` prints netmasks as hexadecimal on macOS: `0xffffff00`. The wildcard form `0.0.0.255` appears in access lists, not in `ifconfig`.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses are in a /27?
questions.why: A /27 has 32 addresses; subtract the network and broadcast addresses to get 30.

questions.q: Which HTTP status means "authenticate first", and which means "authenticated but not allowed"?
questions.why: 401 means credentials are missing or invalid; 403 means the server understood who you are and refuses anyway.
SSH refuses private keys that group or others can read. 600 (or 400) leaves access to the owner only.

questions.q: Which key combination inserts the last argument of the previous command in zsh?
questions.why: Alt+. (Esc then a period) inserts the last word of the previous line, and repeating it cycles further back in history.

questions.q: Why does `pip install requests[socks]` fail in zsh?

options.text: zsh treats the square brackets as a glob and finds no match
the quote characters are missing from the package name
extras only work inside a venv

questions.why: Unquoted `[socks]` is a glob pattern, so zsh stops with `no matches found`. Write `'requests[socks]'`.
